title: Aurelia Health — Dedicated inference capacity strategy discussion
transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-03-28 15:00 UTC — Duration 48m. Recording started. Attendees listed above.

[00:00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone, thanks for carving out time. Jordan from Redwood — I'll be the AE on this. Priya, our SE, is on the call to dig into the perf and ops details.
[00:00:10] Michael: Hi Jordan, Dana, Omar, Sofia here. We're trying to figure out if we go hosted, reserved / dedicated, or private for some regulated inference workloads. Short background: we run clinical triage and summarization models on patient notes, so data residency and encryption are blockers for hosted in some workflows.
[00:00:30] Jordan: Totally. Priya, should I hand it off?
[00:00:33] Priya: Yeah, I'll jump in. Thanks Michael. Maybe start with a quick sketch of current traffic and SLA expectations?
[00:00:40] Dana: Sure. Right now we have two main inference pipelines: realtime triage (sub-500ms target) and batch summarization (offline, tolerant to minutes). Realtime is small footprint — about 120 qps peak across our API from the app, but it's spiky — e.g., during morning surge it goes up by 6x for 10–15 minutes.
[00:01:05] Omar: To add, our token distribution is variable: triage prompts are short (avg 200 tokens) but we have occasional long-context summarizations up to 2k tokens. We care about tail latency (95/99).
[00:01:20] Priya: Good, that's helpful. A couple of immediate tradeoffs we'll call out: reserved/dedicated gives you capacity isolation to handle spikes predictably, and avoids noisy neighbor issues, but you need to size for peak or rely on burst/fallback policies. Hosted can be simpler, cheaper for lower steady state, but public control plane and data egress may be concerns for regulated data. Private (VPC/on-prem) gives the strongest controls but is heavier to operate.
[00:01:45] Sofia: Our security team asked about SOC2, KMS integration, and audit logs. Also whether we can keep patient data in our VPC — we can't send PHI to a shared public endpoint.
[00:01:57] Jordan: Redwood has SOC 2 Type II and supports customer-managed KMS for Private and Dedicated contracts; Dedicated can be configured with a private endpoint in a VPC peering setup so data never traverses public internet depending on the option. We'll surface the exact network topology in the follow-up doc.
[00:02:15] Michael: When you say "burst" — how deterministic is that? If we size for baseline 20 GPUs equivalent and then burst to 40 for mornings, what's the SLA around provisioning?
[00:02:25] Priya: Two things: reserved capacity is reserved and available immediately in the pool you buy. For burst we provide a configurable burst window that can use spare capacity in the region — that's not guaranteed like reserves, but we can also architect a warm-burst pattern where you keep small warm pods or cross-region fallback to another capacity tier. Typical ramp for cold allocation is minutes; warm-prefetch can get you sub-60s scale-ups.
[00:02:48] Omar: Minutes is... borderline. For triage we really need sub-2s for launches. Is warm-prefetch just autoscaling policies that keep a minimal set of warmed kernels?
[00:02:56] Priya: Exactly. The runtime supports warm-standby replicas with persistent KV cache priming and memory mapped weights, which brings startup to seconds. There's an ops cost for keeping those warm instances, so that's part of the cost/latency tradeoff.
[00:03:10] Dana: What about model variants? We might use a quantized 4-bit variant for cost savings during peak and a full FP16 for highest-quality triage. Can Redwood route between them?
[00:03:20] Priya: Yes — routing policies can fall back to cheaper or higher-latency variants automatically. You can set thresholds (latency, cost, error rate) to trigger routing changes. The KV cache isn't compatible across some model variants, so there is cache warming cost on fallback.
[00:03:34] Michael: Network isolation — can we have a private ingress so requests always originate inside our VPC?
[00:03:38] Jordan: For Dedicated we offer a Private Connect option that establishes a peered endpoint — requests ingress via your VPC, and we provide an egress path that can be limited. For Private (on-prem) we can host entirely inside your network. We'll capture the options with diagrams.
[00:03:52] Omar: Let's talk sizing. If we map 120 qps average to GPU count, how would you recommend sizing for our mix of short/long prompts and the morning 6x surge?
[00:04:03] Priya: Quick ballpark approach: simulate token/speed. For short prompts (~200 tokens), an A100-class GPU (or A10G depending on model family and sequences) can handle ~X qps in our perf profiles. We'll run a tailored benchmark; but from experience, for a 6x surge brief window, many customers do a base reserved pool sized for 1.5–2x steady state and rely on warm burst capacity for the remainder. So if steady is 120 qps, baseline reserve might target 180–240 qps equivalent.
[00:04:33] Dana: That 1.5–2x rule of thumb is helpful. But we need to know cost delta between keeping warm instances vs buying more reserved GPUs.
[00:04:41] Jordan: We'll include a cost model in the follow-up — per-GPU reserved rate vs warm-standby cost (usually represented as partial vCPU/GPU hours for kept warm replicas) and the cost of burst usage when using shared capacity.
[00:04:52] Sofia: Security question — audit logs: can we ship token-level logs to our SIEM? PHI gets redacted upstream, but we want request/response hashes, latencies, and error traces.
[00:05:02] Priya: Yes, Redwood Console supports export of observability events to your S3/CloudWatch/BigQuery with redaction and hashing options. For PHI we typically recommend token redaction at the app layer plus sending structured telemetry only.
[00:05:17] Omar: Compliance / data residency — if we choose Dedicated in a US region, is that considered "data stays in-region" or do control plane operations still touch other regions?
[00:05:26] Jordan: Dedicated compute can be pinned to a region and we support a private control plane option for enterprise contracts so control plane talk is also regionalized. We'll clarify which operations still hit global services.
[00:05:36] Michael: Can we run some POC with a minimal dedicated pool for two weeks to validate latency and burst?
[00:05:42] Jordan: Absolutely. Typical POCs we do are 2–4 weeks with a dedicated reservation trial or a Dedicated trial with reduced commit. We'll scope metrics, SLOs, and a deck of benchmarks.
[00:05:52] Dana: On the POC, we'd like a golden set of prompts to measure quality regressions when switching quantized variants. Also an eval harness to detect hallucination rates.
[00:06:02] Priya: We have Redwood Optimize eval integrations; we can ingest your prompts and produce perf + quality matrices. We'll also run a delta analysis between the full model and quantized variant.
[00:06:12] Omar: Operationally, how are rollouts handled? We need canary, percentage-based traffic, and instant rollback.
[00:06:18] Priya: Redwood supports canary and A/B rollouts by traffic percentage, and automatic fallback policies if errors exceed thresholds. Rollout controls are in the Console and expose circuit-breaker heuristics. Rollout changes propagate within seconds for routing rules, though actual model instance spin is subject to your warm/cold policy.
[00:06:33] Sofia: Any limits on KV cache size or multi-tenant cache concerns? We want per-tenant isolation for context windows in triage.
[00:06:41] Priya: KV cache is per-deployment and can be scoped per-customer/tenant with encryption. For very strict isolation we'll recommend per-tenant dedicated slices — which increases overhead but guarantees no cross-tenant caching.
[00:06:54] Michael: What's the typical lead time for provisioning 8–16 GPUs dedicated? We have procurement cycles that prefer longer commitments.
[00:07:02] Jordan: For Dedicated, once the contract is signed, provisioning of reserved pools in a region is typically hours for allocation if we have capacity; if capacity is constrained it can be days. For larger or specialized hardware we recommend confirming capacity early. We'll provide lead-time SLAs in the contract.
[00:07:19] Omar: Do you support HSM-backed KMS for key material?
[00:07:22] Jordan: Yes, we integrate with customer-managed KMS including HSM via supported providers; we'll surface specifics for your KMS vendor.
[00:07:29] Dana: Is there an option for on-prem (air-gapped)? We have a handful of hospitals with strict compliance that require on-prem inference.
[00:07:36] Priya: We offer Private (on-prem) packages; they are heavier to install and support but meet air-gap needs. There's also a hybrid approach where we keep control plane minimal and run inference inside your data center.
[00:07:46] Michael: Let's get into failure modes: if a reserved pool suffers a region outage, what are typical failovers?
[00:07:52] Priya: The pattern we advise is multi-region pools with cross-region fallback. If primary pool loses capacity, traffic routes to secondary region or to a lower-cost hosted fallback variant. We also have graceful degradation policies to reduce model size automatically under severe capacity constraints.
[00:08:07] Omar: That cross-region latency might break our 95p target for triage. How do customers usually handle that?
[00:08:12] Priya: Typically they keep minimal standby capacity in-region (warm-standby) sized for critical traffic that must hit SLOs, and use cross-region only for less-latency-sensitive workloads or during prolonged outages.
[00:08:23] Sofia: For pricing, can you give high-level reserved vs burst numbers so procurement can ballpark spend?
[00:08:29] Jordan: High-level: reserved capacity is priced by GPU-month with discounts for annual commit. Warm-standby is priced as fractional reserved hours and burst usage billed at market/shared rates. We'll send a tailored spreadsheet with model profile and estimated token/hour.
[00:08:44] Michael: Ok — desired outcomes from our side: validate we can hit 95/99 latency for triage in-region, confirm the quantized fallback doesn't significantly change decision quality, and ensure full audit/KMS controls for PHI. Timeline: pilot in April, procurement sign-off early May for Dedicated reserve starting June.
[00:09:00] Jordan: Sounds good. We'll propose a POC scope and SLOs.
[00:09:03] Priya: Quick technical note — for the POC we will need a representative traffic replay and golden prompt set. If you can provide a masked tokenized sample, we can run the bench.
[00:09:13] Dana: We'll prepare a 48-hour replay of typical traffic plus morning surge patterns.
[00:09:16] Omar: Also include our telemetry pipeline endpoints for observability exports.
[00:09:20] Jordan: Great. Any competitive alternatives you're evaluating?
[00:09:24] Michael: We're also looking at HyperscaleCloud AI endpoints and an open-source self-hosted stack (PerfServe) evaluated internally. Concerns with Hyperscale are cost and data residency; self-hosted is tight on ops bandwidth.
[00:09:36] Priya: Makes sense. We'll outline where Redwood sits on the cost/ops spectrum and how Dedicated reduces ops burden vs fully self-hosted while keeping more control than pure hosted.
[00:09:45] Sofia: A couple of smaller questions — can you restrict model uploads and prevent third-party model access under a Dedicated contract?
[00:09:52] Jordan: Yes, RBAC controls can restrict model access; Dedicated pools are isolated so other tenants can't access your models. We'll show the console UI for RBAC in the follow-up.
[00:10:03] Dana: Ok, last quick thing — are there throttles for token per-second per key? We want to enforce per-tenant quotas.
[00:10:09] Priya: Yes, per-key rate limits and token-based quotas are supported. We also expose per-route quotas in the Console.
[00:10:18] Michael: That covers most of it. Wrap up next steps?
[00:10:22] Jordan: Recap: Redwood will deliver a POC proposal (scope, SLOs, cost model) and a network/security topology doc. Priya will run an initial perf baseline and propose sizing for 120 qps steady with morning surge patterns. You'll provide replay and golden prompts.
[00:10:36] Dana: We'll get those to you by EOD Monday.
[00:10:39] Omar: Procurement will need an outline of lead times and contract terms.
[00:10:42] Jordan: We'll add lead-time SLAs and a draft Dedicated term sheet.
[00:10:46] Michael: Thanks all.
[00:10:47] Jordan: Thanks — we'll follow-up with calendar invites for a kickoff POC meeting. Recording stopped.
summary: Discovery call with Aurelia Health Tech to evaluate Dedicated capacity for inference. Discussed traffic patterns (120 qps steady, 6x morning surge), latency SLOs for realtime triage, batch summarization needs, security (SOC2, KMS, VPC), warm-standby vs reserved sizing, model variants and quantization fallbacks, POC scope and timeline (pilot Apr, procurement May, reserve Jun). Agreed Redwood to send POC scope, cost model, network diagrams, and run perf baseline after customer provides masked replay and golden prompts.
